Spotify Crackdown: 12-Month Bans for Family Plan Sharing As Users Find Workaround
10 photos
Photo: Bogdan Popa/autoevolution
Spotify has decided to enforce its household location policy for Family plan holders, this time with another check that makes it harder for users to bypass it. However, a workaround has already been found, though it’ll probably be patched quite fast, as the subscription sharing crackdown is gaining traction.
While Netflix has pretty much pioneered the rule that says that members of a Family plan should be part of the same household - and therefore have the same IP when they connect to the service - this approach came back into the spotlight earlier this year after a massive crackdown launched by Google for YouTube Premium Family account holders.
Google has started restricting access to YouTube Premium for Family users unless they live at the same location as the administrator. While users complained that a family doesn’t necessarily have to live under the same roof - and recommended that Google rename this plan to YouTube Premium Household - the verifications included a demotion to the ad-supported tier.
The same is now happening with Spotify, which so many of us use to listen to our favorite tunes while driving, only that the demotion also includes a 12-month ban for users who aren’t part of the same household as the account owner.
Photo: Spotify Spotify has started conducting a series of checks, asking members of Family plans to confirm that they are part of the same household.
The verification is done with a QR code that appears on the account holder’s phone. The plan manager needs to open the QR code from the Manage screen of the Your Premium section, while the user who needs to verify the account must scan this code with their camera.
Spotify explains that the verification is successful only if the two are in the same place, and reveals that once you get the verification request, you have 7 days to complete it. Otherwise, you’ll be demoted to a free plan - meaning that you’ll start hearing ads - and get a 12-month ban for Spotify Family and Duo. You can get other plans though, including the individual account.
Photo: Spotify Several users have confirmed in the last few days that they received this verification request. Just as expected, many have started looking for loopholes, and the most obvious thing most people tried was to screenshot the QR codes and send them to the rest of the group to complete the verification.
This method doesn’t work, as the QR codes are refreshing every 3 seconds, so you must scan the codes in real time to complete the verification.
A workaround has already been found . Users video call each other from other devices, showing their screens with the QR codes on camera and allowing the rest of the group to scan them as if they were together.
Photo: Spotify Surprisingly, the method appears to work, despite Spotify clearly stating that “both the manager and the member need to be in the same place to complete the scan.” There are obvious ways to circumvent this restriction, considering the verification probably takes place via the IP of the connected devices, and VPNs are the most obvious. However, the method seems to work even without being in the same location.
It’s probably a matter of time until Spotify comes up with a patch for this method, so overall, subscription sharing is becoming significantly more difficult, even for people who were part of the same family.
In the United States, Spotify Premium costs $12.99 for individual accounts and $18.99 for the Duo, which allows for 2 premium accounts. Spotify Premium is available for $21.99 per month, with access for up to 6 accounts, meaning the cost per account drops to just $3.66.
Spotify states that the Family plan is available only for “family members residing at the same address.”
Photo: Spotify Users blast Spotify for enforcing this rule since families don’t always have to be living together.
“I have shared my Spotify Family Plan with my actual family for about 7 years now. For the last 6 of them, I’ve lived nowhere close to them. Last night I got this message,” someone wrote on reddit. “In the same boat, I’ve got two brothers on mine that don’t even live in the same state as me,” someone else added.
However, it doesn’t look like everybody is getting the new re-verification email, as several users explained on reddit that they’re also sharing their accounts with other family members who don’t live under the same roof, and everything is still working correctly. This could be just an experiment for now, as Spotify hasn’t publicly announced the crackdown on subscription sharing, but we should hear more about this shortly if it gains traction.
There’s also a chance that Spotify is just enforcing the re-verification for a number of accounts that it flagged for various reasons, though without further data, it’s impossible to tell what exactly is happening. Let me know in the comments box after the jump if you, too, received the re-verification email.

Bracing for patent losses on its cornerstone product Darzalex, Genmab has bet its future on three cancer programs that will deliver pivotal readouts in quick succession.
Genmab faces an unprecedented situation. Nearing the loss of a revenue source that accounts for 90% of its sales, the company is approaching arguably the largest cliff that any company has ever faced in the pharma industry, Tahamtan Ahmadi, chief medical officer and head of experimental medicines at Genmab, told BioSpace .
And a series of readouts this quarter could foreshadow whether the company will grow beyond the cliff. Two clinical wins earlier this month have set the stage with two more readouts still expected by the end of the year.
Today, Genmab relies heavily on royalties from Darzalex, its Johnson & Johnson–partnered cancer drug whose U.S. patents expire in 2029. Genmab lost cases that could have softened the drop in revenues as these patents run out, creating a steep cliff.
The biotech’s Darzalex revenues could fall from about $3.3 billion in 2028 to under $1 billion by 2031, and to roughly zero by 2032, Raghuram Selvaraju, managing director of Healthcare Equity Research at H.C. Wainwright, told BioSpace by email. Despite that, the analyst believes Genmab can emerge from the trough years of 2029 and 2030 in a strong position.
“We think Genmab has more than enough horsepower under the hood to overcome the almost total loss of revenue from Darzalex,” Selvaraju said. “Genmab’s ability to weather this challenge depends on three wholly owned or partnered oncology assets.”
The company recently shared positive data on two of the three assets. In the first week of October, Genmab reported Phase 3 findings from the AbbVie-partnered Epkinly in first-line lymphoma that analysts said could potentially set “the new standard of care” in this indication and posted “durable and clinically meaningful” Phase 2 results for the antibody-drug conjugate (ADC) rinatabart sesutecan (Rina-S) in ovarian cancer. Genmab expects Phase 3 Rina-S data this year, but Selvaraju now sees data on the third asset, petosemtamab, as the only “binary event risk.”
Lymphoma
AbbVie, Genmab’s Epkinly sets ‘new standard of care’ in first-line lymphoma in Phase 3
AbbVie and Genmab’s bispecific antibody blew analyst expectations out of the water with a 51% improvement in progression-free survival when used alongside a standard frontline regimen in diffuse large B cell lymphoma—potentially setting up a battle with Roche’s Polivy.
October 6, 2026
·
3 min read
·
Tristan Manalac
Read more
Genmab’s big bet
Genmab acquired petosemtamab, a bispecific antibody targeting EGFR and LGR5, last year in its $8 billion takeover of Merus. Among Genmab’s three key assets, “petosemtamab matters the most,” Selvaraju said. That view reflects a sales ramp that could make the bispecific a blockbuster by 2029, the year Darzalex’s U.S. patents expire, as well as possible launches in additional indications.
The lead indication for petosemtamab is head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC). Genmab expects to share results from the Phase 3 LiGeR-HN1 trial in patients with first-line HNSCC by the end of the year. In May 2025, Merus reported a 63% overall response rate (ORR) in a Phase 2 study, far surpassing the 19% Merck’s Keytruda achieved in the Phase 3 KEYNOTE-048 study—a result noted by both Selvaraju and Genmab’s Ahmadi.
Achieving a 40-point or greater improvement in ORR, a co-primary endpoint in the Phase 3 trial, “would support accelerated approval and fast uptake,” Selvaraju said. Beyond that, Genmab would need to show that the increased response rate translates into improved progression-free (PFS) and overall survival (OS), the latter the study’s other primary outcome measure. PFS is a secondary endpoint. Ahmadi outlined how ORR could predict PFS and OS.
“If you have a dramatic ORR difference, and the durability is good, it almost has to translate into a statistical or near-statistical PFS difference. And then, of course, it has to translate into separation in the OS curves, because otherwise it would have a safety liability,” the CMO said.
Business
Genmab and AbbVie’s Epkinly win, a rush of deals, Sarepta’s turnaround hopes, more
New data for Genmab and AbbVie’s bispecific antibody Epkinly wowed analysts and could set the partners up for an expanded approval in diffuse large B cell lymphoma; deals have flowed steadily this week, including Novartis’ nearly $8 billion bet on mRNA drugs with China’s Abogen Biosciences; and could Sarepta Therapeutics turn things around from last year’s annus horribilis?
October 7, 2026
·
2 min read
·
Jef Akst
Read more
ADC nears key readout
LiGeR-HN1 is one of two remaining Phase 3 readouts for Genmab assets this year. The biotech also plans to share data from RAINFOL-02 , which is testing its FRα-directed ADC Rina-S in platinum-resistant ovarian cancer (PROC).
The readout is “relatively risk-mitigated because of the positive Phase 1/2 RAINFOL-01 data in PROC,” Selvaraju said. The Phase 1/2 clinical trial linked Rina-S to a median PFS of 9.5 months, hitting a secondary endpoint. AbbVie’s rival FRα-directed ADC Elahere achieved a median PFS of 5.6 months in the Phase 3 MIRASOL trial.
Chemotherapy is the control treatment in RAINFOL-02. Based on the earlier data on Rina-S and chemotherapy, the RAINFOL-02 readout could be “very positive on PFS and potentially even on OS,” Ahmadi said. A positive PFS outcome—the trial’s primary endpoint—is “highly likely, with interim OS success (a higher bar) being possible in an upside scenario,” Guggenheim Securities analysts said in an Oct. 4 note to investors.
Analysts are also looking for Genmab to replicate the breadth of efficacy seen in the Phase 1/2 trial, when the biotech reported activity in patients with low or no FRα expression. Securing a label across FRα levels would double the addressable population compared to Elahere, Selvaraju said. The analyst sees the FRα labeling terms as the variable that will determine the slope of the ramp for Rina-S sales.
The competitive landscape amplifies the value of launching and growing Rina-S quickly. Rina-S is part of a wave of ADCs that use topoisomerase-1 (TOPO-1) inhibitors to treat ovarian cancer. Once a patient progresses after receiving one TOPO-1 ADC, they are unlikely to benefit from another treatment with the same payload, Ahmadi said. The importance of becoming the first-choice TOPO-1 ADC is encouraging speed and secrecy.
“We are not pre-announcing these studies anymore. We basically make them public at the time the first patient gets dosed,” Ahmadi said. “It is competitive and everybody’s looking over everybody’s shoulder and copying everybody’s strategy.”
Competing commercially
Victories in LiGeR-HN1 and RAINFOL-02 would establish petosemtamab and Rina-S alongside Epkinly as drugs that can power Genmab through and beyond the Darzalex cliff. Yet positive data will only be a step toward the sales Genmab needs to mitigate the loss of royalties from the drug. Genmab also needs to achieve regulatory and commercial successes, and it is facing those challenges solo.
The market “is still a little bit skeptical” about Genmab’s prospects in this respect, Ahmadi acknowledged. Genmab is entering “a hypercompetitive environment” and biotechs always face questions about whether they can compete commercially with larger rivals, he added.
Ahmadi sees Epkinly’s success as evidence that Genmab can rise to the challenge. Working with AbbVie, Genmab has turned Epkinly into a challenger to Roche, a company that “owned” the market for 25 years with Polivy and Rituxan, Ahmadi said. Through that process, Genmab has built commercial and operational capabilities that could benefit petosemtamab and Rina-S.
“We’ve been beating [Roche’s Columvi] quarter for quarter for quarter,” Ahmadi said. “I think that is a little bit unappreciated: how good we have become in running these trials, speeding up development, and how competitive we already are as a company.”

All-New Mercedes-Benz C-Class Electric Arrives in the Land Down Under, Kicks Off at AU$105,700
16 photos
Photo: Mercedes-Benz
The compact premium executive all-electric revolution has reached Australia as far as Mercedes-Benz is concerned, and this is the starting price for the all-new, first-ever Mercedes-Benz C-Class Electric – the C 400 4Matic version, that is.
Mercedes-Benz has been making the C-Class since 1993, when it was introduced as the replacement for the 190 model, and it’s been around for five generations before the premium German automaker decided to also make a battery electric compact executive car with the same name. The Mercedes-Benz C-Class Electric was initially teased during the 2025 Munich Motor Show launch event for the Mercedes-Benz GLC Electric cousin, and debuted in April 2026 in a single version, the C 400 4Matic.
The combustion version, by the way, is still around, and the W206 iteration introduced in early 2021 also got a mid-cycle refresh procedure in August 2026 to bring it up to snuff with the rest of the range and the Electric variant. Now the latter is going on sale in Australia, starting on October 20, 2026, in the same version as in other regions – the C 400 4Matic .
It “brings together expressive design, exhilarating electric performance and an immersive digital interior, while retaining the comfort and everyday usability that have long been the hallmark of the Mercedes-Benz C-Class.” Designed from scratch as an all-electric automobile, the C-Class Electric has the new visual identity of EVs for the brand, with the grille featuring 1,050 illuminated dots, an integrated central star and an illuminated surround.
There are animated lighting sequences for the grille, along with the three-pointed star LED daytime running lamps and the double-circle LED star taillights. In Australia, the AMG Line and the Night Package are standard, complete with 20-inch AMG multi-spoke light-alloy wheels. Inside, the AMG Line continues the theme, and there’s also the Keyless-go Convenience Package among other perks.
The cockpit has the latest Mercedes-Benz Operating System (MB.OS) connected to the Mercedes-Benz Intelligent Cloud, and features the fourth generation of MBUX, an AI-powered MBUX Virtual Assistant that combines technology from ChatGPT, Microsoft Bing and Google Gemini to understand natural speech, plus Mercedes-Benz Navigation with Electric Intelligence.
The MBUX Superscreen comes standard, featuring a 10.25-inch digital instrument cluster, a 14-inch central touchscreen and a dedicated 14-inch front-passenger display under the same glass surface, and buyers also get the standard AMG Line Sports Seat Package or a Burmester 3D surround sound system, among other things. All for AU$105,700, which equates to about $73,850 at the current exchange rate.
The powertrain uses a dual-motor electric drivetrain setup with 360 kW and 800 Nm, which is 483 hp and 590 lb-ft of torque, plus 4Matic all-wheel drive for a sprint to 100 kph or 62 mph in exactly four seconds. There’s a 94 kWh usable lithium-ion battery pack with a WLTP rating of up to 753 km (468 miles) of range, and the 800-volt platform enables DC fast charging at up to 330 kW.

Mars Mission Not Actually Targeting Mars Lifts Off From Japan, Will Return With Samples
13 photos
Photo: JAXA
In the six decades or so that have passed since humanity sent its first spacecraft, Mariner 4, to planet Mars, there have been around 50 more or less successful missions to the Red Planet. A few of them have come close to the planet’s two Moons, Phobos and Deimos, but none have actually targeted them directly. Until now.
For a while now, the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) has been working with NASA and a number of international companies to put together a mission to these two moons. The spacecraft that resulted from this work is called the Martian Moons eXploration (MMX), and it was just sent on its way to its targets.
As announced over the weekend, the spacecraft lifted off from the Yoshinobu Launch Complex at the JAXA Tanegashima Space Center on board an H3 rocket, embarking on a journey that, in the summer of next year, will end with it reaching its target.
MMX is not simply a survey mission, although it will do plenty of that as well. Its main focus is to send back to Earth, around the year 2031, soil samples from Mars’ larger Moon, Phobos. Their arrival and subsequent study here on Earth could shed more light on how the two moons came to be, and possibly into the past of our own planet.
There are two main theories Earth scientists rely on when it comes to the formation of Phobos and Deimos: they were either born as asteroids that somehow got entangled in Mars’ gravitational pull and turned into its moons, or they came to be as a result of asteroid impact ejecta being shot up into orbit billions of years ago.
It is hoped that the MMX will prove one of these theories and disprove the other, and in the process give us a better understanding of how the solar system’s inner planets have acquired most of their water and organic compounds.
After arriving in Martian orbit, the spacecraft will spend about a year orbiting and studying them from afar. Then, it will send a lander down to the surface of Phobos and try to collect some samples.
There are two main instruments on board tasked with this mission. The first one, the C-sampler, has been designed by JAXA as a coring tool that’s meant to dig into the Moon’s surface and collect samples from underneath the surface.
The second one is called a P-sampler, and it’s a tool imagined by Blue Origin-owned Honeybee Robotics. A pneumatic tool by trade, it uses pressurized nitrogen gas to blow off regolith from the surface and capture it inside a collection chamber. A sort of glorified vacuum cleaner, if you will.
Aside from these two samplers, the spacecraft also carries an instrument called the Mars-moon Exploration with GAmma rays and Neutrons, or MEGANE. That would be a spectrograph designed to measure the neutrons and gamma rays emitted from the moon’s surface, trying this way to get a better sense of what the surface is made of from a chemical point of view.
JAXA didn’t say how much surface material it hopes to collect from Phobos, but whatever it is, it will be shared with the international community.

Server CPUs
NVIDIA BlueField-4 STX Server for CMX at OCP 2026 2 Large
At OCP 2026, we saw the new NVIDIA BlueField-4 STX Server for Context Memory (CMX). Partners had been asking for this, and NVIDIA delivered. Onboard, we have a lower-cost design than the dual-Vera setup we saw previously. Let us take a look at the new board.
NVIDIA BlueField-4 STX Server for CMX at OCP 2026
For context, this is the previously shown BlueField-4 DPU. That one, pictured below, is a dual Vera CPU setup, each with SOCAMM memory, plus four ConnectX-9 SuperNICs. NVIDIA calls this a DPU, but it is clearly more costly than a BlueField-1 or BlueField-3, which are much smaller and lower-power devices. For partners looking at building storage platforms, the below is more akin to a dual CPU server than a traditional DPU.
NVIDIA BlueField-4 STXf
At OCP 2026, multiple partners showed off the BlueField-4 STX server for context memory (CMX). Here is the much smaller card, which still uses high-density connectors for PCIe and system connectivity.
NVIDIA BlueField-4 DPUs encompass both NVIDIA Grace and Vera CPU cores, but this one looks like a Vera package. That is a very substantial CPU. To be clear, this is not like the embedded-class CPUs that we typically have seen in DPUs previously. This is more like having a high-end single-socket server platform.
NVIDIA BlueField-4 STX Server for CMX at OCP 2026 5 Large
Another interesting feature is that the boards at OCP 2026 are using SOCAMM memory, so these should be relatively easy to put either a heatsink or a liquid cooling block on top of it.
NVIDIA BlueField-4 STX Server for CMX at OCP 2026 3 Large
Onboard, there is an M.2 slot. Usually these are for OS drives, but if you saw our recent Inside the Secretive AWS Networking Lab, the M.2 SSDs there are being used for log devices.
NVIDIA BlueField-4 STX Server for CMX at OCP 2026 4 Large
This may seem like a small feature, but it means NVIDIA designed this less like a traditional motherboard replacement and more like something that is easy to assemble automatically.
NVIDIA BlueField-4 STX Server for CMX at OCP 2026 1 Large
Something that may not immediately hit you if you are looking at photos is just the size of this board. A soldered CPU and LPDDR5X here, over traditional DDR5 DIMM slots, give NVIDIA a platform where the “motherboard” is roughly the size of an Intel DMR 16-channel socket or a 16-channel AMD EPYC Venice platform.
Final Words
This is just a neat platform. It almost feels like NVIDIA needs some brand between the Vera server line and the traditional BlueField DPU line. Something notable that we did not see on the boards shown at OCP 2026, or at least in our photos of them from various booths, is an NVIDIA ConnectX-9 SuperNIC. We expected that, but did not see it on this board. For context memory platforms, a single Vera versus a dual Vera makes this a lower-cost platform, and that will likely help the STX/ CMX systems come to market as the price of NAND has been rising meaningfully over the past year.

Ford Kuga Crossover Hit With Safety Recall Over Wiring Harness Damage
29 photos
Photo: Ford
The Ford Kuga has been recalled yet again for an issue that can end in a vehicle fire. After high-voltage battery issues, now it's a specific harness that may lead to a fire. Referred to as 17052R by the German KBA, the latest recall involves 35,545 units worldwide, namely crossovers whose instrument panel harness can chafe until it either kills the drive system or shorts out with a bang.
The main harness is the wiring spine behind the dashboard, carrying the signals and feeds that make any modern vehicle actually run. Chafed loom is one of the oldest failure modes in the industry, and you can blame plenty of things for it: heat cycles, excessive vibration, a bracket edge that wasn't rounded off properly, and so forth. The climax depends on which harness wire gives up first.
In this case, subject Kugas can either lose propulsion at high speeds, increasing the risk of a crash, or start burning. Neither Ford nor the German watchdog said what the harness rubs against, only that damage can happen. The build window for the suspect vehicles runs December 20, 2024, through July 10, 2026.
That's 18 months of production at the Valencia plant in Spain, which is essentially the whole recent output of the Escape's European brother. The fix comes in the form of cable ties, protective caps, and some tape. Service technicians are required to strap the harness back, cap what needs capping, wrap the wearing surfaces, and restore clearance between the loom and whatever it may touch.
Reading between the remedy and the recall condition, it's easy to understand that someone messed up the routing. Only 42 units of the 35,545-strong population were originally registered in Germany, which is Europe's largest market for new vehicles. For the full picture of the Kuga's year, Ford recalled nearly 167,000 units earlier this year over a high-voltage battery fire risk on the plug-in hybrid.
Photo: Ford The KBA is aware of zero fire reports, injury reports, or property damage resulting from the aforementioned issue. For a model on its second electrical safety recall of the year in the German market, zip ties and rerouting is about the best possible outcome after the high-voltage battery fiasco from earlier in 2026.
As far as we know, Ford of Europe plans to keep the current-gen Kuga in production through the end of 2029 at the Valencia plant in Spain. Kuga PHEV series production continues despite a July 2026 joint venture agreement between the Ford Motor Company and Chinese automaker Geely, which will see the introduction of two new crossovers to the facility by decade's end.
One of them will be a Bronco family model, whereas the Geely crossover is understood to come in the form of a multi-energy vehicle. Whether the Bronco-branded model will ultimately replace the Kuga in Europe as the Bronco Sport replaced the Escape in the United States of America, we simply do not know yet.
Currently one of the most popular C-segment crossovers in Europe, as well as one of the most popular plug-in hybrid SUVs in the Old Continent, the Kuga clocked a little over 105,000 registrations in 2024. That figure made it the 29th best-selling model in the European space, with the Kuga PHEV finishing 2024 as the second most popular plug-in hybrid of the bunch.

Don’t do it. I know you’re tempted to click the photos in the gallery, but don’t do it. Because if you do, there’s a good chance you’ll walk away instantly, without getting a chance to discover this 1971 Dodge Challenger.
I admit that most people would consider it a wreck, a rust bucket, or a flower pot, but I’m with the seller this time. A restoration is still “technically possible,” the man states, and I don’t think this is wishful thinking. This Challenger is rough, but really now, we’ve all seen many cars in horrible shape getting a second chance, so why shouldn’t this once-Plum Crazy specimen have the same fate?
That’s right, you’ve heard it correctly. This Challenger left the factory wearing the eye-candy Plum Crazy , but the car was the subject of a series of unfortunate decisions that turned it into the pile of rusty metal that you can see in the photos here.
Photo: eBay seller poundshort It’s no secret that the 1971 Challenger was struggling with an unwelcoming market, mainly due to the insurance costs and regulations aimed at models with big muscle. The dropping sales were barely surprising, but the level of the collapse wasn’t necessarily easy to digest.
The Challenger fell from over 83,000 cars sold in the previous year to only 29,883 units.
Dodge tried to find a way to deal with the new market trends, so the Challenger was available only in three series and four models.
The two-door hardtop was the configuration that dominated the series, accounting for over 23,000 orders. This made sense, considering it was also the most affordable, carrying a base price of $2,858 for the version fitted with a six-cylinder engine - yes, a six was still offered, but most Challenger buyers agreed that this didn’t make much sense; fewer than 2,000 cars got a six.
The R/T accounted for 4,630 orders, while the convertible was the rarest with 2,165 buyers.
Photo: eBay seller poundshort Dodge offered a wide variety of engines, but the Challenger was already prepared for big changes for the following model year. This was the last year for the Hemi, so 191 was the last opportunity to pay $790 for the massive 425-horsepower upgrade.
The Challenger lineup included 18 colors, with five high-impact configurations . Hemi Orange and Plum Crazy were and still are the most desirable.
Unfortunately, this Challenger no longer wears the original Plum Crazy treatment.
“The second owner bought this car and painted it blue,” the seller reveals. That’s a sad change, not just because Plum Crazy was such a fantastic color, but also because it pushed the car further away from its original setup. The blue finish certainly doesn’t look as good as Plum Crazy, though it’s fair to admit that its current condition doesn’t help either.
I don’t think it makes sense to dissect its condition because it’s pretty clear that this Challenger requires extensive work in every single regard. There’s a lot of rust, but the owner says there are also solid sections.
“It has some rare and nice parts, including the whole convertible top mechanism, which is very solid, and intact rear window glass,” they reveal.
Photo: eBay seller poundshort An engine is no longer in the car, but this isn’t necessarily bad news. It’s been sitting for so long and in horrible conditions that an engine would have only been seized.
“I was told that it was originally a 318 engine car,” the seller says. So you’re not missing anything special, though the factory 318 unit would have helped the bravest souls out there keep the car original.
As for the car’s overall condition, we should just blame the rainy days for it.
“It sat outside since 1985, and while it was covered by tarps, they long since decayed, and the car was exposed to weather and moisture. The owner passed away, and I purchased it from his widow,” the seller explains.
That’s why the rust damage is massive. The floor pan is no more, and the seller notes that “the frame and the underbody are not visible.”
Photo: eBay seller poundshort This is a major project, by all means, and my recommendation is that you go there in person to see it with your eyes if you somehow believe it’s worth your time and money. The owner lives in Epping, New Hampshire, and you’ll obviously need a trailer to take it home because there’s no chance you’ll get this car on its wheels otherwise. The front wheels are frozen, but the rear ones still turn.
As for the price, it’s pretty clear that you can’t pay high dollars for this Challenger. That’s why the owner decided to let a no-reserve auction decide the price, though the starting bid could end up keeping people away.
To join the digital fight, you must pay at least $4,976, and so far, nobody has done so, despite over 20 users adding the Challenger to their watchlists. The auction ends in 5 days.
